messages.text: There both down
I'm H., HeliumDeploy's technical specialist. Let me get up to speed on both units.
Used the heliumdeploy-ops-knowledge skill

Sorry to hear that, Jeff. Let's find out what "down" means on each one, and we'll start with the simplest fact.

1. Plug one in and look at the unit: does anything light up at all (screen on, LEDs, fans spinning)?
2. Tell me the same for the second one.

If both are completely dead with no screen and no fans, say so and also tell me whether they are on their original power bricks or something else. If they do power up but are not hashing, a photo of the screen or the web UI home page is the fastest thing you can send me.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)
I've opened the photo. Let me check that exact code before I say anything about it.
Searched the web · NerdQaxe++ "VOLTAGE PROTECTION" "Guru Meditation" 60008000
Searched the web · ESP-Miner NerdQaxe overheat_mode "Guru Meditation" voltage p
Nothing yet on that exact code. Checking the firmware source and Harlo's site now.
Searched the web · shufps ESP-Miner-NerdQAxePlus "voltage protection" alert cod
Read harlolabs.com
Read github.com/shufps/ESP-Miner-NerdQAxePlus/issues/707

Thanks, that photo tells me a lot. What I can see on it:

- NerdQaxe++, BM1370 chips, web UI at 192.168.1.232 so the ESP32 side is alive and on Wi-Fi
- Red banner: VOLTAGE PROTECTION, Guru Meditation #····
- 0.0 GH/s, 0.062 W, 28 C

The near-zero wattage means the firmware has cut the ASIC voltage rail and is refusing to turn the chips on. That is a protection trip, not a dead board by itself.

I could not find that exact code (#····) in the NerdQaxe firmware issues or release notes, and I will not guess at a code's meaning. So two things from you before I go further:

1. In the web UI at 192.168.1.232, what firmware version does it show?
2. Does the second unit show this exact same message, or something different? A photo of its screen too if you can.

Also useful: are both units on their original 12V bricks, and are they sharing one outlet or power strip? Two units tripping at the same time often points at what they are fed from.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)
Used rma verdict

Second photo opened. That one reads:

- VREG OVERHEATED, Guru Meditation #····
- Same IP 192.168.1.232, same BM1370, 0.0 GH/s, 0.062 W, 29 C

So each unit stops at a different point but with the same end result: the firmware refuses to bring the ASIC voltage rail up, which is why the power reads 0.062 W instead of a few hundred.

On the codes, so you know where this comes from: #···· (VREG overheated) is documented in the NerdQaxe firmware tracker on GitHub, issue 707, on the same Rev 6.1 board. There the voltage regulator reported about 128 C for a fraction of a second the instant the rail was enabled, the firmware cut it to 0 V and never retried, even though the regulator was sitting at under 30 C. That matches your 29 C reading exactly. #···· I still cannot find documented anywhere, and I am not going to invent a meaning for it.

Three things and I can close this out:

1. Both photos show the IP 192.168.1.232. Is the second photo really the second unit, or the same one on a later boot?
2. The firmware version, from the web UI at that IP or from the settings screen.
3. Pull the DC barrel plug right out, wait a full minute with no power at all, plug it back in and tell me what the screen says on that cold boot.

A clear photo of the serial number sticker on each board would also save a round trip later.
Both on there own power supply

Good, that rules out a weak brick. That is a Mean Well LRS-350-12, 12 V 29 A, 350 W, far more than a NerdQaxe++ needs.

But that model has something the stock bricks do not: a 115 V / 230 V AC input selector slide switch, right next to the AC terminal block. The yellow label on it is the warning about it. If that switch sits on 230 V while you are on 120 V mains, the unit still powers up and the screen lights, but the 12 V rail sags as soon as the ASIC tries to draw current, and the board trips its own protection instead of hashing. Two units failing the same week on two supplies of the same type makes a common cause like that worth ruling out before anything else.

So, carefully:

1. Unplug the AC cord from the supply completely. Do not touch or unscrew the terminal block, there is exposed mains there.
2. Look at the small slide switch beside the terminals: is it set to 115 V or 230 V? Tell me what each of the two supplies reads.

And I still need the firmware version from the web UI at 192.168.1.232, plus whether that second photo was really the second unit. Those two answers plus the switch position should settle this.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)

That settles the supply side: the selector on that one is set to 115 V, correct for US mains, so it is not a 230 V mis-set. I can also see the output voltage trim screw (the recessed pot) and the barcode on the case.

One step left, and it gives me everything at once. Open http://192.168.1.232 in a browser on the same network and send me a screenshot of the dashboard page.

That page shows three things I need:
1. The firmware version
2. The input voltage the board is actually seeing on its 12 V rail
3. The A. voltage and the current error state

If the input voltage reads around 12 V and the board is still cutting the rail with VREG OVERHEATED at 29 C, the supply has done its job and the fault is on the board itself. If it reads well off 12 V, that trim pot or the supply is the culprit and that is a different fix.

If the page will not load, tell me that instead and send a photo of the second unit's screen plus its serial sticker.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)

Thanks. That confirms the board has done nothing since boot: 0.00 Gh/s against 4896 Gh/s expected, 0 shares, efficiency infinite, and 0 best difficulty since boot (the 8.9G is just the all-time record it remembers).

What I still need is further down that same page. Scroll to the bottom of the dashboard and send me that part. It shows:

- Firmware version
- Input voltage and ASIC voltage
- ASIC temperature and VR temperature

That block is the deciding evidence. If input voltage is sitting near 12 V while ASIC voltage is 0 V and VR temp is normal, the supply is doing its job and the board is cutting its own rail, which is a board-level fault and I will take it to the team with everything we have gathered.
(The customer sent this photo without a message.)
Used rma verdict
I've recorded my findings and handed the chat back.
